items.title: Can penalties imposed on insolvent developer be recovered from homebuyers as CIRP costs? Supreme Court answers
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday held that time extension charges imposed on an insolvent developer cannot be recovered as Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) costs from homebuyers [ Granite Gate Properties v. NOIDA & Ors. ]. A Bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran set aside an order of the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) which had directed a Committee of Creditors (CoC) comprising homebuyers to pay the time extension charges imposed by the New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) on housing projects stalled since 2016. The Court said the homebuyers and the new developer were being made to bear the consequences of the original developer’s default. items.title: ‘Leave granted’ became ‘Chutti swikriti’: Justice KV Viswanathan highlights promise and risks of AI in law
items.summary: Supreme Court Justice KV Viswanathan on Thursday highlighted the pitfalls of translation of legal documents and judgments using Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools. He recalled how use of AI to translate his first judgment to Hindi resulted in the familiar judicial expression 'leave granted' being translated to “Chutti swikriti”, effectively telling the litigant that their leave had been sanctioned. 'Leave granted' when used by the Supreme Court means that a special leave petition before it has been admitted and converted into a full-fledged appeal and the Supreme Court is required to deliver a reasoned judgment. A special leave petition can otherwise be dismissed at the threshold without giving any reasons. Justice Viswanathan said that after delivering his first judgment as a Supreme Court judge, he was curious to see how it would read in Hindi. The judgment began, as many Supreme Court judgments do, with 'leave granted'. The translated version, however, read ' chutti swikriti' . “ Meaning your leave is sanctioned ,” he quipped. He was speaking at the inaugural session of the Gujarat High Court Arbitration Centre Arbitration Week 2026, when he used the anecdote to highlight both the promise and risks of AI in adjudication and arbitration. The three-day Arbitration Week brings together judges, lawyers, government representatives, businesses, arbitral institutions and international practitioners under the theme “Three days, three stakeholders, one vision”. Justice Viswanathan also narrated how Harvey AI had reportedly been asked by an American law firm to predict the questions US Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch might ask at an upcoming hearing of a case. Of the 11 questions generated by AI, Justice Viswanathan said, 10 were eventually asked. The judge said AI could substantially reduce the time spent on document review, translation, legal research and organisation of voluminous records. Courts and arbitral tribunals could even explore using AI to prepare a statement of undisputed facts in fact-heavy cases, which parties could then verify, he suggested. However, he cautioned that AI could fabricate legal authorities and propositions and could also pose serious confidentiality risks. The emerging principle, he said, was that AI could assist an arbitrator or lawyer but responsibility for reasoning, judgment and the eventual award could not be delegated to a machine. items.title: Hebbal Lake tunnel: HC seeks technical presentation amid concerns over water flow
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court on Thursday, September 3, adjourned to next week the hearing on a PIL challenging the proposed short tunnel project at Hebbal Lake. It also directed the authorities to arrange a technical presentation to show that the project will not affect the lake’s inflow or outflow. A division bench comprising Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice KS Hemalekha said a presentation by an engineer could address the petitioners’ concern that the project could drain the lake. Appearing for petitioners RK Guruprasad and two others, advocate Sneha Nagaraj said lake land had been diverted for the tunnel project. She argued that the construction would obstruct the lake’s inlet and outlet, and said this was reflected in documents available with the authorities. Advocate General Shashikiran Shetty, however, told the court that the project would not affect the lake’s inflow or outflow. He agreed to arrange a technical presentation by an engineer explaining how the project would ensure that the water body’s flow remains undisturbed. The petitioners have sought the quashing of the Detailed Project Report (DPR) titled “Short Length Transitory 3-Lane Bi-Directional Vehicular Underpass connecting Hebbal Flyover Junction to Veterinary College via GKVK campus premises”. The DPR was prepared pursuant to the revised final draft report of September 2025. They have also challenged provisions of the Karnataka Tank Conservation and Development Authority (Amendment) Act that reduced buffer zones around lakes, calling them unconstitutional. The petitioners have further sought the striking down of Rule 24 of the Bengaluru Metropolitan Land Transport Authority (BMLTA)Rules, which exempts the project from the prior approval required under the BMLTA Act. HC seeks GSI report on Lalbagh In a separate PIL concerning Bengaluru’s proposed twin-tunnel project, the High Court directed the state government to place before it a Geological Survey of India (GSI) report on the Peninsular Gneissic Complex at Lalbagh. The direction came after Bengaluru South MP Tejasvi Surya, who appeared as counsel, urged the court to call for the report. The division bench adjourned the hearing on a PIL filed by Dr Adikesavalu Ravindra, theatre personality Prakash Belawadi and others to September 10. items.title: A POCSO case involving a mining baron that Chennai police tried to close
items.summary: Last year, in October, the Chennai police had received a pen drive containing the visuals of a minor being sexually assaulted. It came to light that the man in the video was an influential mining baron in his early 80s. However, in a major travesty of a process, the police tried to close the case. The investigation was reopened in July 2026, and on August 29, the police arrested Rangaswami Veeramani, founder of GEM Granites and the GEM Group of Companies, along with Mahendra Simhan, MD of Gem Software Solutions, and his wife, Shanthi, who are accused of facilitating the alleged offences at their house. The three were produced before a court and remanded in judicial custody. While the police had first attempted to drop the investigation claiming that the child’s identity could not be confirmed, a Special Court judge for Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) refused to accept the police’s closure report, forcing the Chennai police to reopen the case. The re-investigation led to the recovery of a gadget containing what is described as the original visuals of the assault from one of the accused’s residences. TNM tried to fill in the gaps of how systemic corruption and lack of will led to the prolonged denial of justice to the child, while the perpetrators remained shielded by power and influence. The pen drive containing assault visuals It was last year, on October 6, 2025, that a child rights activist approached the Anti-Vice Squad of the Chennai police and handed over a pen drive containing a video that showed a minor girl being sexually assaulted. According to the police, the activist said that an unidentified person had visited her office and handed over a pen drive containing the footage and a letter. She also told the police that a note that came with the pen drive said that the man in the video was GEM Granites founder R Veeramani and the assault was happening at the house of Mahendra and Shanthi. Police sources told TNM that the CCTV footage had a timestamp dating back to 2019. No progress for a year According to the police, upon receiving the video footage and the complaint, an FIR was registered against Veeramani and Shanthi under the POCSO Act and sent to the court. In October 2025, investigating officers apparently made several attempts to identify and locate the minor, but there was no breakthrough.
